vignette:
He is 21, a young European man who now drives a city bus on early morning and late afternoon routes. Most passengers see only a quiet driver with steady hands and a habit of checking his mirrors more often than necessary. Over several meetings, a more complicated story emerges, one that begins before dawn in a military convoy and continues into the ordinary streets he navigates now.

He joins the military just after finishing school. He likes the structure, the sense that there is a clear next step, and the promise that he will become tougher than he feels. He is one of the youngest in his unit and spends a lot of time watching the older men, copying how they move and talk. At first, he enjoys the routine and the camaraderie. He learns to keep his bunk neat, to move quickly when called, to laugh off discomfort. He feels proud wearing the uniform. His mother worries, but he tells her he will be fine.

The event he returns to again and again happens during a convoy. It is hot, bright, and strangely quiet in the minutes before everything changes. He remembers the road ahead looking almost still, dust hanging in the air. Then there is an explosion near the lead vehicle, followed by shouting and a burst of noise so overwhelming that he cannot separate one sound from another. He feels his body moving before his mind catches up. He is out of the vehicle, heart hammering, trying to locate where the fire is coming from. He sees one of the men he has eaten beside, joked with, and tried to impress lying injured in a way that does not make sense at first glance. He remembers the smell most vividly: fuel, metal, dirt, something burnt. He remembers trying to do what he has been trained to do while feeling, with humiliating clarity, that he is no longer inside himself. Everything becomes both painfully sharp and far away.

Afterward, he tells himself he should be able to handle it. Other men seem to keep going. He keeps going too. He does what is required, but sleep changes almost immediately. When he closes his eyes, the road appears again. Sometimes it is the explosion exactly as it happened; sometimes the scene shifts and he is the one trapped, unable to move, hearing others call for help. He wakes drenched in sweat, already standing before he is fully awake. Loud sounds begin to get to him. A dropped metal tray, a door slamming, a motorcycle backfiring nearby—each one sends a jolt through him before he can think. He starts scanning roadsides and rooftops automatically. Even when he knows he is safe, his body does not seem convinced.

By the time he leaves the military, people around him think he is quieter, but they do not know how much work it takes for him to appear normal. He moves back home and takes a job driving buses, partly because it is practical and partly because he likes the idea of having a route, a timetable, a defined start and end. Yet the job places him inside some of the same conditions that unsettle him most: being responsible for others, watching the road constantly, anticipating danger before it happens. He studies every unattended bag at a stop. If a passenger stands too close behind him, he feels his shoulders tighten. Roadworks, debris in the lane, cars stopped unexpectedly ahead—these can pull him into a state of instant alarm. On bad days, a piece of tire tread in the road is enough to make his chest clamp and his hands go cold on the wheel.

He does not tell colleagues much. He says he is tired, that he prefers to keep to himself. When other drivers complain over coffee about rude passengers or traffic, he nods without joining in. He avoids crowded pubs because he cannot relax with his back exposed. He sits near exits in cafés and watches doorways without meaning to. Friends from school have mostly stopped inviting him out after he cancels repeatedly. He is single, though not because he does not want closeness. He says it is hard to explain to someone why he might go silent halfway through dinner because a smell, a sound, or a flash of light has taken him somewhere else.

What troubles him almost as much as the memories is the guilt. He thinks about the injured man from the convoy and reviews his own actions in endless loops, asking whether he moved quickly enough, whether he missed something, whether fear made him into the kind of person he never wanted to be. He knows, in a factual way, what others have told him—that he responded as anyone would under fire—but the knowledge does not settle the feeling. It lives in him anyway.

In the present, his world has narrowed. He works, goes home, and keeps his room orderly in a way that feels less like preference than necessity. Sleep comes late and lightly. He startles easily, trusts slowly, and feels older than 21. Still, he shows up to work on time, keeps his bus on schedule, and apologizes softly when passengers see only a reserved young driver. Beneath that restraint, he is carrying a road that has never fully ended.
